paragraphs: Editorial checklist | Fixed occupation 0436, funeral home managers, corresponds to 11-9171.00. Its 23 core tasks cover family arrangements, personnel and facilities, and pricing and operations. Use for self-questioning only, not hiring scores; verify actual qualifications and authority separately.

Paper exercise | Complete the H/V2 fictional three-ceremony farewell-hall operations exercise. Check assumed itemized quotations, single-hall and individual scheduling conflicts, inventory, and V1/D2/R versions. Full materials, answers, four work samples, and a seven-day plan appear in the pathway. Do not issue actual quotes, handle remains, collect fees, sign contracts, or publish.

Context signals | Occupational questionnaire: 100% daily telephone use, 92% daily face-to-face contact, 85% constant contact, and 74% substantial decision freedom. Use context to explore communication and organizational tasks, not to judge a particular personality's competence.

Tradeoff suggestion | 54% report extremely serious error consequences and 59% extreme importance of accuracy. The 58% for conflict and 48% for unpleasant people refer to at least monthly but not weekly, not accident rates. 67% work more than 40 hours weekly; 55% report regular and 45% irregular schedules. These cannot be transferred to individuals or China.

Exploration method | Independently recalculate quotations, schedules, and inventory for the three ceremonies in H/V2; retain versions and Q's unresumed status. This reveals paper methods but cannot verify actual grief communication, business, hygiene, or legal competence. No experienced outsider's sign-off is required.

Direct answer | Editors organize the work around family arrangements, pricing and operations, and personnel and facilities. All 23 duties remain represented from the occupational profile; the management title does not exclude on-site tasks.

Occupational definition | O*NET-SOC11-9171.00 Funeral Home Managers, with the fixed Chinese occupational title translated as funeral home managers; plan, direct, or coordinate funeral home service resources, including pricing and facility management. All 23 tasks are core: discuss funeral details with and comfort families; schedule funerals, burials, and cremations; send death certificates to legally authorized signers; supervise compliance; direct embalming, service, registration, and cosmetic staff; maintain state paperwork, tracking documents, and inventory; sell services and negotiate prearrangement contracts; adjust services; handle complaints, legal inquiries, and payment negotiations; set staff goals and schedules, recruit and train; set prices and credit terms; review financial performance and reduce costs; oversee administration and repairs; set marketing and financial goals; conduct community outreach; evaluate suppliers; research markets; and promote sales. Management and professional handling roles may be combined. The title grants no unrestricted handling or signing authority; verify jurisdictional and institutional requirements.

entries: Family communication and arrangements | Confirm needs, farewells, and burial | Discuss and arrange funeral details with the deceased person's family or friends, including obituary wording, casket selection, and ceremony plans, and provide advice and comfort.

Scheduling and supervision | Ceremonies, burials, and cremations | Schedule funerals, burials, or cremations and supervise funeral service operations for compliance with applicable policies, regulations, and laws.

Teams and personnel | Direction, scheduling, recruitment, and development | Direct and supervise embalming, cosmetic preparation, funeral service, death registration, and makeup staff; schedule working hours, interview and hire new employees, and identify skill-development needs.

Pricing and sales | Prices, sales, and prearrangements | Set prices or credit terms for funeral products or services, sell funeral services, products, or merchandise to clients, and negotiate prearranged funeral service contracts.

Compliance and records | Permits, files, and inventory | Complete and maintain state-required paperwork, tracking documents, product inventories, and other records; deliver death certificates to medical facilities or offices for legally authorized signatures.

Operations and markets | Finance, performance, community, and marketing | Review financial statements and sales or activity reports to identify cost reduction or service improvement opportunities; set and track marketing, sales, or financial goals; plan and implement service-program changes and sales promotions; attend or host community events; and assess supplier quality and cost-effectiveness.

Team and public | Teamwork is extremely important for 79% and very important for 21%; public interaction is extremely important for 79% and very important for 14%.

Pressure and conflict | 57% experience time pressure daily, 25% at least weekly but not daily; 58% encounter conflict and 48% unpleasant people at least monthly but not weekly.
Environment and vehicles | 83% work in controlled indoor environments daily, 79% in enclosed vehicles daily; 56% work outdoors exposed to weather at least weekly but not daily.
Hygiene and protection | Disease exposure 46%, contaminants 49%, heat or cold 55%, routine protective equipment 47%, and hazardous conditions 34% all refer to at least weekly but not daily. Another 36% report disease exposure daily; 46% is not an infection rate.
Physical demands and schedules | 61% stand about half the time, 50% sit about half the time, 49% work in close proximity; 67% work more than 40 hours weekly, 24% work 40 hours. Mainland China | Funeral regulations revised in 2025 took effect on 2026-03-30. Article 25 reserves remains collection and transport, storage, embalming, cosmetic preparation, and cremation to funeral homes; Article 26 requires a death certificate for collection and transport; Article 28 requires a certificate and confirmation for cremation and at least 90 days of video from key areas. Obvious discrepancies in cause of death must be reported to public security under Article 26. Managerial appointment does not authorize every entity to offer the five services or sign death certificates. The 2025 infectious disease law took effect on 2025-09-01; Article 71 distinguishes sanitary handling and notification for deaths from Class A diseases/anthrax and other infectious diseases, rather than applying one protocol universally. Chinese fees | NDRC Price [2026] No. 108 differentiates basic/nonbasic services and institutional nature. No charges outside the list, without required disclosure, or contrary to policy; clients cannot be restricted from bringing their own urns. Trial price-display rules effective 2026-05-31 require consistency across channels in Articles 4/15, disclosure of each service in packages in Article 5, and funeral home nature, rates, pricing forms, bases, and reductions in Article 16. Under Article 24, when consumption precedes settlement, choices and prices must be confirmed before service and settlement receipts must list items and prices. Articles 28/29 prohibit undisclosed charges and fraud; Article 6 requires written agreement for personalized services. Verify local lists and rates separately; managers cannot price arbitrarily. US FTC | The rule applies to funeral providers that both sell or offer funeral goods and provide the two categories of services, including relevant prearrangement agents; holding a funeral-home license is not the sole test. Provide a take-away GPL during face-to-face discussions of service choices or prices; give accurate price information by telephone, without a universal requirement to mail a GPL. Packages cannot replace required itemized prices. Embalming charges require checking the three categories of conditions involving state law, explicit prior permission, or attempts to contact, rather than declaring all charges prohibited. Federal law does not mandate embalming. Retain price lists for at least one year after last distribution and selected-goods-and-services statements for at least one year after the arrangements conference; check state law separately. Information boundary | PIPL6/13/19 covers minimum necessity, lawful basis, and retention periods. Apply statutory sensitive-information conditions and applicable separate-consent rules under 28/29; names, contact details, family relationships, and grief are not automatically sensitive, though health information may qualify. Article 49 allows close relatives to exercise relevant rights for their own lawful and legitimate interests unless the deceased arranged otherwise during life; check security and access under 51. Under 47, do not directly delete information before statutory retention expires. Verify publication and external-provision procedures separately; do not invent family consent.
Check personnel, facilities, and records; handle specific matters under jurisdictional authorization.

Editorial comparison | Managers emphasize institutional operations; attendants specific on-site work; morticians professional handling and arrangements; medical managers healthcare institutions; social and community managers programs; and general operations cross-functional work. Roles can overlap or be combined; verify actual authority by jurisdiction and institution.

Core concept of adjacent roles | Most roles in the same group or nearby aim to provide dignified services and care during vulnerable moments involving life and health while ensuring compliant organizational operations. They differ in responsibility level and outputs: overall funeral home operations, pricing, and compliance; on-site services and execution support; professional handling of remains; healthcare or social-service institutional management; or cross-functional business operations.

This occupation's core purpose | Working with family needs and authorization and institutional resources, translate funeral services into executable arrangements, personnel, venues, schedules, prices, and records within legal and institutional authority: confirm family choices and costs, schedule and allocate resources, check permits, credentials and price documents, supervise services, and archive business and compliance records so services are measurable and lawful.

Main subjects and bases of adjacent roles | Funeral attendants follow daily workflows, family requirements, and institutional operating standards. Morticians, undertakers, and funeral arrangers follow funeral operating standards and state practice requirements. Medical and health services managers follow clinical and medical laws and institutional policies. Social and community service managers follow social-service policies and program rules. General and operations managers follow business goals, contracts, budgets, and compliance systems.

This occupation's main subjects and bases | Family needs and authorization; ceremony, cremation or burial arrangements; staff, venues, equipment and suppliers; prices, contracts and permit documents; and business and compliance records. Work follows applicable funeral service and consumer protection laws, such as the US Funeral Rule and local state practice requirements or mainland China's funeral service fee and price-display rules, personal information protection requirements, and institutional authorization, approval, and governance procedures.

Occupational definition | O*NET-SOC11-9171.00 Funeral Home Managers, with the fixed Chinese occupational title translated as funeral home managers; plan, direct, or coordinate funeral home service resources, including pricing and facility management. All 23 tasks are core: discuss funeral details with and comfort families; schedule funerals, burials, and cremations; send death certificates to legally authorized signers; supervise compliance; direct embalming, service, registration, and cosmetic staff; maintain state paperwork, tracking documents, and inventory; sell services and negotiate prearrangement contracts; adjust services; handle complaints, legal inquiries, and payment negotiations; set staff goals and schedules, recruit and train; set prices and credit terms; review financial performance and reduce costs; oversee administration and repairs; set marketing and financial goals; conduct community outreach; evaluate suppliers; research markets; and promote sales. Management and professional handling roles may be combined. The title grants no unrestricted handling or signing authority; verify jurisdictional and institutional requirements.

Core processes of adjacent roles | Funeral attendants mainly execute daily workflows and provide on-site services and facility support. Morticians, undertakers, and funeral arrangers emphasize professional operations and paperwork for embalming, cosmetic preparation, funeral arrangements, and family communication. Medical and health services managers emphasize clinical, nursing, healthcare operations, quality, and compliance management. Social and community service managers emphasize program design, social-service delivery, resources, and performance management. General and operations managers emphasize cross-functional business goals, budgets, procedures, and performance.

This occupation's core process | Confirm family needs and authorization; schedule ceremonies, cremations or burials and allocate resources, staff and suppliers; coordinate remains collection, transport, and handovers to authorized personnel; check prices, contracts and permit documents; supervise on-site services, complaints, and settlement; archive business and compliance records and review performance. Every step requires institutional documentation that supervisors, authorities, and auditors can review.

Main outputs of adjacent roles | Funeral attendants deliver procedural on-site services, facility support, and handover records. Morticians, undertakers, and funeral arrangers produce professional results and documents for handling and cosmetic preparation of remains and ceremony arrangements. Medical and health services managers produce healthcare institutional operations, quality, and compliance outcomes. Social and community service managers produce social-service program, resource, and performance outcomes. General and operations managers produce cross-functional business operations, financial, and performance outcomes.

This occupation's main outputs | Arrangement forms reflecting family needs and authorization and itemized quotations; ceremony, cremation or burial schedules and venue and staffing allocations; remains collection, transport, and authorized-personnel handover documentation; permits, credentials, fee documents, and death-certificate signature records; inventory, tracking documents and state-required paperwork; complaint and after-sales records; and marketing, sales and financial goals and performance-review results.

Responsible parties in adjacent roles | Responsibility in the same group and adjacent roles is usually defined by institutions, professional principles, industry standards, and regulatory rules. Accountability commonly extends to institutions, families, clients, authorities, and the public.

Responsible party | Managers bear their appointed operational management responsibilities. Professional-service, pricing, and information responsibilities also require checking the actual entity, jurisdiction, and institutional scope; titles do not replace authorization.

Adjacent authority | Verify jurisdictional and institutional conditions separately for on-site, professional, medical, social-program, and cross-functional roles. Tasks may be combined, but similar emphases do not confer direct authority.

Authority check | China's five professional services are reserved to funeral homes; fees require checking listed standards and disclosure; death certificates follow legally authorized entities. Managerial appointment does not replace professional authority.

Comparison boundary | Adjacent and current duties may overlap. Verify practice requirements, institutional scope, and hiring conditions independently; titles and career comparisons are not qualification determinations.

Conclusion boundary | Quotation, scheduling, inventory, and performance records can show operational methods. Still distinguish facts, assumptions, and pending confirmations; paper work samples do not establish professional qualifications or actual business competence.

Pre-entry verification notes | Check the following six items individually during applications and before starting, rather than inferring duties and authority from titles or promotional wording. Base findings on written recruitment information, employment contracts, job descriptions, and institutional policies, and continue confirming after joining. This page lists verification directions, not any institution's official requirements.

Verification notes | Similar titles can hide major duty differences: some emphasize family services, ceremony arrangements, and on-site operations; others sales, prearrangement contracts, and targets; others pricing, compliance, finance, and personnel. Institutions also differ in authority over pricing, approval and release, and remains handling.

01 Actual duties and authority boundaries | Check whether the role truly manages service arrangements, staff, venues, schedules, prices, and compliance, or mainly involves sales, reception, on-site execution, or operational support. Check approval paths for quotations, fee commitments, approval and release, permit documents, and remains handling, plus pause and escalation procedures for unauthorized or abnormal matters.

Information boundary | PIPL6/13/19 covers minimum necessity, lawful basis, and retention periods. Apply statutory sensitive-information conditions and applicable separate-consent rules under 28/29; names, contact details, family relationships, and grief are not automatically sensitive, though health information may qualify. Article 49 allows close relatives to exercise relevant rights for their own lawful and legitimate interests unless the deceased arranged otherwise during life; check security and access under 51. Under 47, do not directly delete information before statutory retention expires. Verify publication and external-provision procedures separately; do not invent family consent.

02 Pricing, permits, and consumer protection | Check whether the institution provides itemized prices, disclosures, reduction policies, and pricing rules under applicable requirements, including the US Funeral Rule and mainland China's funeral service fee and price-display rules. Check prohibitions on undisclosed charges, misleading pricing, tied sales, and unauthorized charges; written records of family choices and prior authorization; verification and documentation procedures for permits, credentials, death registration and remains handover; and the scope and basis of deceased persons' and families' information collection, system access, and retention.

US preparation | O*NET's occupation-specific new-hire requirements questionnaire reports 50% associate's or two-year degree, 26% high school or equivalent, and 15% postsecondary certificate, not workforce education; remaining proportions are not invented. Zone3/SVP6 to below 7 is a grouping; one to two years of training within the group is not a universal duration for every job in this occupation. BLS lists typical associate's education, less than 5 years of related experience, and on-the-job training None, which does not prohibit training. The combined OOH scope indicates most employers/state laws require age 21, at least two years of higher education, supervised training and examinations. Verify specific states and institutions; do not import Chinese entry thresholds.

03 Education, training, and qualifications | Check whether funeral service or business administration education or a postsecondary certificate is required; whether state practice qualifications, minimum age, supervised training and examinations are required; whether pricing, compliance, consumer protection, personal information protection, safety and hygiene training is provided; and what qualifications and institutional authorization are required for remains handling, death registration, and cremation.

Income check | The national 78,790 dollars is US employee wages, not Chinese wages or self-employed business returns. Specific contractual pay components and standby hours were not sampled; check written conditions. Insufficient evidence: Exact Chinese occupational classification, national wages and employment, city recruitment contracts, and wage structures were not obtained. NBS industry and US data cannot fill the gaps. Bounded searches do not establish that statistics do not exist.

04 Pay, working hours, and contract definitions | Check offered pay components: base pay, performance or sales commission or business bonuses, standby, night-shift or holiday allowances, overtime pay or compensatory leave, and vehicle and travel allowances. Check working hours, standby, weekend and holiday schedules, probation and business or sales assessment measures, and whether work involves outstation assignments, rotations, or cross-region operations.

Verification notes | Interfaces with families, on-site teams, remains-handling personnel, finance, legal staff, suppliers, and authorities determine pricing, permit, authorization, and responsibility boundaries and must be clear in advance.

05 Interface authority with families, on-site teams, remains-handling personnel, and authorities | Check authority for family communication, fee commitments, and complaints; duties and handovers with attendants, morticians, embalming and cosmetic staff; verification and approval paths with finance, legal and compliance; supplier and contract-worker evaluation and acceptance; and referral paths for price disclosures, missing permits, external personal-information provision, major complaints, and legal inquiries.

Verification notes | Traceability and documentation requirements for services, prices, permits, fees, and complaints determine management intensity and accountability. Establish version, modification, archiving, and access rules in advance.

06 Records, disclosures, and traceability | Check versioning, modification, archiving, retention, and access rules for family needs and authorization, itemized prices and disclosures, ceremony, cremation or burial arrangements and on-site services, remains collection, transport and handover, permits, credentials and fee documents, inventory, tracking documents and state-required paperwork. Check duties to provide evidence and cooperate during price disclosure, complaints, and audits.

More suited to people willing to do on-site, physical, and driving work in bereavement settings, follow procedures, and report within authority; this occupation emphasizes pricing, personnel, compliance, and operations.

Core work and outputs: Welcome, guide and accompany mourners; arrange caskets, wreaths and lighting and assist with casket closure; support funeral vehicles, processions and parking; maintain and recover venues and equipment; and retain handover documentation for remains collection, transport, encoffining and cosmetic preparation. Professional operations emphasis | Morticians/undertakers/funeral arrangers emphasize professional operations and arrangements; managers emphasize institutional operations. Roles may be combined; verify state qualifications and institutional scope separately.

More suited to people focused on professional remains handling, cosmetic preparation, ceremony arrangements, and direct family communication who are willing to obtain practice qualifications; this occupation emphasizes institutional operations and compliance management.

Core work and outputs: Embalming, cosmetic preparation, encoffining, funeral arrangements and ceremony execution; confirming family needs and religious and cultural preferences; permit, credential and remains-handover paperwork; on-site management and quality checks. Outputs are professional results and documents for remains handling, cosmetic preparation, and ceremony arrangements.
Morticians, undertakers, and funeral arrangers (Morticians, Undertakers, and Funeral Arrangers)

Key distinction: Medical and health services managers manage clinical care, nursing, quality, compliance, human resources, and budgets in healthcare institutions, serving patients and healthcare staff. This occupation manages funeral home services, resources, prices, and facilities for bereaved families and communities. Their legal, risk, and authorization systems differ.

More suited to people focused on healthcare operations, clinical quality, healthcare teams, and medical laws; this occupation emphasizes funeral services, prices, consumer protection, and facility management.

Core work and outputs: Healthcare institutional operations and clinical and nursing quality; compliance, accreditation and patient safety; personnel, budgets and performance management; collaboration with healthcare staff and authorities. Outputs are healthcare operations, quality, and compliance management outcomes.
Medical and health services managers (Medical and Health Services Managers)

Key distinction: Social and community service managers manage social-service programs, public resources, case services, and funding for communities and vulnerable groups. This occupation manages funeral home operations, pricing, facilities, and personnel for bereaved families and consumers.
More suited to people focused on social-program design, service delivery, resources, and funding management; this occupation emphasizes commercial service operations and consumer protection.

Core work and outputs: Social-service program design, budgets and funding; service quality, case and referral management; relationships with communities, government and partner institutions; performance and compliance reports. Outputs are social-service program, resource, and performance outcomes.
Social and community service managers (Social and Community Service Managers)

Key distinction: General and operations managers handle cross-functional business goals, budgets, procedures, and performance across industries and products. This occupation's operations concern funeral home services, resources, prices, and facilities and are subject to specialized funeral and consumer protection laws.
More suited to people focused on cross-functional operations, costs, and process improvement who can move across industries; this occupation emphasizes specialized funeral laws and family services.

Core work and outputs: Business goals, budgets and forecasts; process, supply chain, quality and cost management; organization, talent and performance management; cross-department collaboration and reporting. Outputs are cross-functional operations, financial, and performance outcomes.
General and operations managers (General and Operations Managers)

subject.summary: Occupational definition | O*NET-SOC11-9171.00 Funeral Home Managers, with the fixed Chinese occupational title translated as funeral home managers; plan, direct, or coordinate funeral home service resources, including pricing and facility management. All 23 tasks are core: discuss funeral details with and comfort families; schedule funerals, burials, and cremations; send death certificates to legally authorized signers; supervise compliance; direct embalming, service, registration, and cosmetic staff; maintain state paperwork, tracking documents, and inventory; sell services and negotiate prearrangement contracts; adjust services; handle complaints, legal inquiries, and payment negotiations; set staff goals and schedules, recruit and train; set prices and credit terms; review financial performance and reduce costs; oversee administration and repairs; set marketing and financial goals; conduct community outreach; evaluate suppliers; research markets; and promote sales. Management and professional handling roles may be combined. The title grants no unrestricted handling or signing authority; verify jurisdictional and institutional requirements.
